h1: The 7 Best Microwaves Under $100 for Small Kitchens, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 microwaves under $100 compared on wattage, capacity, power levels, safety lock and controls, from Toshiba to Commercial Chef.
summary: The TOSHIBA 0.9 cubic foot, 900 watt microwave is the one to buy if you want real power from a budget unit, because it is the only model here that clears 700 watts. The Chefman 0.7 cubic foot gives the best feature set for a small kitchen, the COMFEE' is the dependable all-rounder, and the Commercial Chef is the simple dial option for anyone who dislikes keypads.
intro: The usual mistake with a cheap microwave is shopping by cubic feet and ignoring watts. Most frozen meals, popcorn bags and soup cups print their cook times for a stronger oven, so a 700 watt unit will quietly run those instructions short, and you end up with a cold centre and a hot edge. Wattage decides how a microwave feels to use every single day.

So this ranking leads with power and then works down through capacity, power levels, defrost options and controls. We reviewed seven countertop models from the listings and spec data, all in the $50 to $100 bracket, and only counted features the listings actually state. Where a number is missing, we leave it out rather than guess.

products.name: TOSHIBA Microwave Oven
products.verdict: The only microwave here that pairs a 0.9 cubic foot cavity with 900 watts.
products.description:
This Toshiba lists a 0.9 cubic foot capacity and 900 watts of power in the $50 to $100 bracket. That is a step above every other model in this ranking, which top out at 0.7 cubic feet and 700 watts.

It takes first place because the extra wattage changes everyday results. At 900 watts, packaged food cooks closer to its printed time, leftovers heat through more evenly, and a mug of water does not take forever. The bigger cavity also lets a standard dinner plate turn freely, which matters because a plate that cannot rotate cooks unevenly. It sits ahead of the Chefman 0.7 because raw power and room beat extra convenience features for most households.

Buy it if the microwave is used several times a day and you want fewer cold spots. Skip it if your counter is very tight, since a 0.9 cubic foot box takes noticeably more room than the compact units below.
products.idealFor: Busy households that use the microwave several times daily.
products.skipIf: Your counter or dorm shelf is very tight.

products.name: Chefman Countertop Microwave Oven 0.7 Cu. Ft.
products.verdict: 700 watts with 10 power levels, Eco Mode, a child lock and a mute button.
products.description:
The Chefman 0.7 cubic foot oven is a black 700 watt unit with 10 power levels, plus Eco Mode, child lock and a mute key. Its price falls in the $50 to $100 range.

It ranks second because the feature list is the most complete among the 700 watt models. Ten power levels let you defrost gently or warm butter without scorching it, which a simple high and low switch cannot do. The mute button is a small thing that matters in a shared flat or a nursery, and the child lock stops a curious toddler from starting the oven. It loses to the Toshiba on raw power, so heating a big bowl takes longer.

Choose it if you want fine control and household safety features in a compact box. Skip it if you prefer the speed of a stronger 900 watt unit.
pros: Ten power levels for gentle cooking
products.idealFor: Households with kids or shared sleeping spaces.
products.skipIf: You want the fastest possible reheats.

products.name: COMFEE' Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 0.7 cubic foot, 700 watt microwave with an Eco Mode and a track record in this size class.
products.description:
The COMFEE' is a 0.7 cubic foot countertop microwave rated at 700 watts, with an Eco Mode, in the $50 to $100 bracket. The listings also show a pearl white finish for the same model family, which helps if you want it to match a light kitchen.

It lands third because it covers the basics with no fuss. It lacks the ten-level control and child lock that put the Chefman ahead, but it does the everyday jobs of reheating, defrosting and popcorn without drama. Eco Mode reduces standby draw, which suits a unit that spends most of its life waiting. Against the BLACK+DECKER below, it earns the nod for the extra mode and the colour choice.

Buy it for a first flat, a bedroom or an office where a no-nonsense microwave is the goal. Skip it if you need a child lock or detailed power levels.
products.idealFor: First flats, bedrooms and offices needing a simple oven.
products.skipIf: You want a child lock or fine power control.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A plain 0.7 cubic foot, 700 watt oven from a brand most buyers already trust.
products.description:
This BLACK+DECKER is a 0.7 cubic foot countertop microwave with 700 watts, priced in the $50 to $100 bracket. The listing is spare, with capacity and power as the headline numbers and nothing else claimed.

That honesty is both the appeal and the limit. It covers a standard job list of reheating, defrosting and basic cooking, and the brand carries enough recognition that replacement and support questions are easy to answer. It ranks fourth because competitors at the same price add an Eco Mode, a child lock or ten power levels, while this one gives no extras on paper.

Buy it if you want a no-surprise microwave and put weight on a familiar name. Skip it if features like a lock or a mute button matter to you.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want a plain oven from a known name.
products.skipIf: You want safety lock or sound controls.

products.name: Farberware 0.7 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: 700 watts with auto cook settings and defrost for people who like a preset button.
products.description:
The Farberware lists 0.7 cubic feet, 700 watts, auto cook settings and a defrost function in the $50 to $100 bracket. The auto cook presets are the draw, because they replace guesswork for items like popcorn, potatoes or a beverage.

It ranks fifth because presets tend to be tuned for typical portions, and the 700 watt power limits how well they handle larger plates. They save time for casual users, but experienced cooks often override them. Compared with the COMFEE' above it offers more guided cooking and fewer eco-minded features, and compared with the Chefman it lacks a documented child lock.

Buy it if you want to press a button and walk away. Skip it if you like to set times and power levels yourself.
products.idealFor: Casual cooks who like one-button presets.
products.skipIf: You prefer to set time and power by hand.

products.name: Chefman Compact Countertop Microwave Oven 0.7 Cu. Ft.
products.verdict: A compact Chefman with 10 power levels, two defrost settings, a child lock and mute.
products.description:
This compact Chefman pairs 700 watts and 10 power levels with a pair of defrost programs, a lock for children and a silence key, all for $50 to $100. It is the same maker as the second-place pick, with a slightly different feature mix.

The two defrost settings are the standout, because defrosting is where cheap microwaves most often cook the edges of meat before the middle thaws. Choosing between modes by weight or time gives you more control. It ranks sixth because it does not list Eco Mode, which the other Chefman does, and because the compact format offers little more capacity than its rivals.

Buy it if defrosting is a regular chore and you want a child lock. Skip it if you already lean towards the roomier Toshiba.
products.idealFor: Cooks who thaw meat and want a child lock.
products.skipIf: You want the extra power of a 900 watt unit.

products.name: Commercial Chef 0.6 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 0.6 cubic foot oven with mechanical dials and a pull handle, no keypad to fail.
products.description:
The Commercial Chef is the smallest and simplest oven here, with a 0.6 cubic foot cavity, 700 watts, mechanical dial controls, six power levels and a pull handle door, in the $50 to $100 bracket.

Dials have a loyal following because there is no membrane keypad to wear out and nothing to program. You twist a knob and it runs, which suits older users and anyone who finds touch panels fiddly. It ranks last because the cavity is the smallest in the group, six power levels give less control than ten, and there is no child lock or Eco Mode in the listing.

Buy it if you want the least complicated microwave you can get. Skip it if you need to heat full-size plates or want presets.
pros: Mechanical dials are easy to use
products.idealFor: Older users and anyone who dislikes touch panels.
products.skipIf: You need to heat full-size dinner plates.

methodology.description: Every model sits in one price bracket, so we scored how much power, space and control each one delivers for that money.

whatMatters.detail: Wattage is the oven's output, and it governs how long food takes. Many packaged meals assume roughly 1,000 watts, so a 700 watt oven needs longer times and more stirring to avoid cold centres. Check the wattage on the listing rather than assuming, and consider the 900 watt Toshiba if you cook from frozen often.

Capacity in cubic feet decides which plates and containers fit. At 0.6 to 0.7 cubic feet, a large dinner plate may scrape the walls and stop rotating, which cooks unevenly. Measure your biggest plate against the internal diameter before buying a compact model.

Power levels let you cook at less than full output, which is how you melt chocolate or thaw meat without cooking the outside. Ten levels, as on the Chefman units, give finer steps than six. Look for dedicated defrost settings too, because they handle thawing by weight or time.

Keypads allow presets and precise timing, while dials are simpler and last longer in many kitchens. The choice depends on who uses it. If a grandparent or a child is the main user, a dial and a child lock are worth more than extra buttons.

A child safety lock prevents accidental starts, and a mute button silences the beeps that wake a sleeping house. Both are small, listed features that cost little to include. Confirm them on the listing, because several of these models do not state either.

faq.q: Will a 700 watt microwave work for frozen meals?
faq.a: Yes, but add time. Package directions are usually written for a stronger oven, so a 700 watt unit needs roughly a third to half longer. Stir or rotate the food partway through to avoid cold spots.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake when buying a cheap microwave?
faq.a: Looking only at the size and ignoring the wattage. A 0.7 cubic foot oven at 700 watts and a 0.9 cubic foot oven at 900 watts are very different in daily use, even though the price bracket is the same.

faq.q: Is the TOSHIBA worth it over a COMFEE'?
faq.a: If you cook from frozen or reheat full plates, yes. The 900 watts and the larger cavity noticeably shorten cook times and improve evenness. For coffee and snacks, the COMFEE' is enough.

faq.q: How do I set up a new microwave safely?
faq.a: Place it on a stable counter with clearance around the vents, plug it into its own outlet if possible, and run it briefly with a cup of water to confirm it heats. Remove all packing material from the cavity first.

faq.q: How do I clean the inside without damaging it?
faq.a: Heat a bowl of water with a splash of lemon juice for a few minutes to loosen splatter, then wipe with a soft cloth. Avoid abrasive pads, which can scratch the interior coating.

faq.q: Can I put metal or foil inside?
faq.a: Generally no. Metal can spark and damage the oven. Use microwave-safe glass or ceramic, and check your manual for any special instructions on foil or metal racks.

finalTake: For most buyers, the TOSHIBA 900 watt microwave is the best choice under $100, because power and a bigger cavity matter more than any extra button. If you want safety and control in a compact box, the Chefman 0.7 cubic foot is the pick, and the COMFEE' is the dependable middle option. The Commercial Chef suits anyone who wants dials and no menu. Check the wattage first and the size second, and the rest is easy.
